summary: Read all 1459 lines of Sahasrabudhe, "Probabilistic combinatorics at exponentially small scales" (arXiv:2512.15077v1; page numbers below are inferred from the 'Copyright' page footers in the txt, line numbers refer to the txt). Seven mechanisms were extracted with their exact estimates and hypotheses. Verdict on transfer to F1-F7: (1) the hub-diagonal pairing (X∘Y)Z^T is literally a weighted codegree (PROVED, one line; CHECKED), but the survey's use of codegrees is the opposite of our situation: there the codegree is SMALL relative to the degree (Δ_2 ≤ Δ/(log Δ)^7) and is used only to bound a quadratic variation for a one-sided existence result, and the "lift" (Thm 3.6) keeps only two scalar statistics; here the pairing has ensemble mean zero (cubic in W; CHECKED on W_off0: per-entry mean 5e-5 against rms 4.8e-3) and its off-diagonal 'bulk' carries n/5 ≈ 205 times the Frobenius energy of its diagonal (CHECKED), which is F2, and F3 says no scalar summary regenerates it, which is exactly what a lift forgets. (2) Conditional exposure + quadratic-variation double count is, at the identity level, the same object as the pinning scheme and the Gram theorem (QV of a function of a process = Hessian × Gram of gradients) but the survey's payoff is a concentration bound while F5 needs the exact trace to 1e-4 relative; the Gram matrix's off-diagonal energy equals its diagonal energy for He weights (‖S_off‖_F² = ‖diag S‖_F² = 4n), so there is no 'codegree ≪ degree' regime to exploit. (3) Klartag's evolving ellipsoid and the Lovett–Meka walk are guided, constraint-sticking processes designed to reach an exponentially rare event; Eldan's path (sec_problem Cor. eldan) is unguided with a deterministic covariance I/(1+t), and Prop. capacity + the measured flat spectrum of the excess second variation show that choosing directions adaptively cannot help because the error is a trace: resemblance is verbal. The one shared skeleton is 'first moment of a count = volume' (Siegel-type Poisson heuristic, line 731) versus 'u(ν)=ν(F) is affine' (Thm defect-path), which is why both are martingale arguments; no estimate transfers. (4) The kink density φ(α)/σ is the Littlewood–Offord concentration function at the FIXED level b=0 (not maximized over b) in the limit ε→0 for a continuous law; CHECKED on net 0 with 131072 inputs: the birth-weighted true small-ball density agrees with φ(α)/σ to ≤0.3% at every layer (≤0.1% with the Edgeworth κ3,κ4 correction), deviating by 5-35% only for |α|>2 where births are negligible. L–O theory gives upper bounds with absolute constants (Thm 4.2: ≤ Cε + e^{-cαn}) for discrete X with an arithmetic (LCD) hypothesis; F6 needs the value itself to 1e-4 relative; the survey itself says the continuous case is 'vastly easier' (line 1132). No transfer. (5) The approximate negative correlation Thm 4.3 has hypotheses (X uniform on {±1}^n, D_α(v) > 16/ε, k ≤ αβn) that are not met, and its Gaussian analogue has the OPPOSITE sign (CHECKED: conditioning on |<X,w_i>|≤β increases the density of <X,v> at 0 by 4%-128% depending on overlap and β). (6) Rank-splitting on singular values (E_k, (4.15)-(4.18)) resembles F3's cocycle 99%-rank only verbally. Net result: none of the survey's estimates applies to F1-F7; the structural identities (codegree, QV/Gram, affine first moment) are exact but already contained in the repo's Theorems, and the survey's quantitative regime (exponentially small probabilities, discrete randomness, one-sided bounds, o(1) relative accuracy) is orthogonal to the regime of the problem (mean-zero cubic functional needed to 1e-3, exact trace needed to 1e-4).

mechanisms.name: M1. Poisson discretization and first-moment degree/codegree counts
mechanisms.statement: Sample a Poisson point process X in [-L,L]^d at intensity λ = d^{d/2-o(d)}, chosen so that the nearest neighbour of a typical point is at distance ≫ log d (closer points deleted). Conflict graph: x∼y iff ‖x−y‖_2 < 2 r_d (r_d = radius of a unit-volume ball); independent sets of G_X are sphere packings. Expected degree E|X ∩ B_{2r_d}(x)| = Vol(B_{2r_d}) λ = 2^d λ =: Δ. Expected codegree E|X ∩ B_{2r_d}(x) ∩ B_{2r_d}(y)| = Vol(B_{2r_d}(x) ∩ B_{2r_d}(y)) λ ≤ 2^d λ e^{−‖x−y‖_2^2/2} ≤ Δ/(log Δ)^{ω(1)}, using ‖x−y‖_2 ≫ log d. Both are first-moment (expectation) computations of counts under a Poisson law; they are the only two statistics retained.
mechanisms.where: §3.3 'Sketch proof - a graph theoretic reduction', p.11, lines 606-641 (λ at line 612, degree at line 627, codegree at line 638).
mechanisms.status: PROVED in the survey (elementary Poisson first moments); the inequality chain for the codegree is stated, with the Gaussian factor coming from the intersection volume of two balls at distance ≫ log d.
mechanisms.relevance_to_F1_F7: Verbal only. The survey's counts are nonnegative with a positive first moment equal to a volume; the information is in the mean. The hub-diagonal pairing of F1/F2 is cubic in the last weight matrix and has ensemble mean zero (PROVED: odd moment of a sign-symmetric Gaussian; CHECKED on W_off0: per-entry mean 5.0e-5 vs per-entry rms 4.78e-3, and the average over the 16 matrices has rms 1.196e-3 = 4.78e-3/√16 exactly as for a mean-zero variable). Everything in our object is at second moment (variance 3n(2/n)^3 per off-diagonal entry); a first-moment/intensity computation of the survey's kind returns zero. This is the same statement as F4's 'Gaussian sketches of the hub index have zero mean on trilinear forms'.

mechanisms.name: M2. 'Lift' from geometry to a graph theorem via (degree, max codegree): Theorem 3.6
mechanisms.statement: Lines 623-624: 'We now would like to "lift" this graph out of its geometric context and think of it only as a graph. But what properties can we hold on to?' The answer is the two scalars Δ and Δ_2. Theorem 3.6: Let G be an n-vertex graph with Δ(G) ≤ Δ and Δ_2(G) ≤ C Δ (log Δ)^{−c}. Then α(G) ≥ (1 − o(1)) n log Δ / Δ, o(1) → 0 as Δ → ∞, with C = 2^{−7}, c = 7. (Triangle counts, the AKS/Shearer statistic, were tried in [49] and only reproduce Rogers' bound; the codegree is the new statistic.)
mechanisms.status: PROVED (in [15], Campos–Jenssen–Michelen–Sahasrabudhe); the survey gives only a sketch (§3.4).
mechanisms.relevance_to_F1_F7: Formal identity, PROVED and CHECKED: for a 0/1 adjacency matrix A, ((A∘A)A^T)_{ik} = Σ_r A_{ir}A_{ir}A_{kr} = |N(i)∩N(k)| is the codegree (checkA: max abs diff 0.0), so the hub-diagonal readout Σ_r X_{ir}Y_{ir}Z_{kr} of F1 is a real-valued, signed codegree between rows i and k through the hub r, and the diagonal Σ_r X_{ir}Y_{ir}Z_{ir} is the degree-type term. But the mechanism points the wrong way for F2/F3. (a) The lift succeeds because the target (a lower bound on α(G)) is one-sided and realization-insensitive, so two scalars suffice; F3 states (measured) that the memory is not regenerable from current statistics and not learnable from per-neuron features, i.e. the memory is precisely what a lift forgets. (b) The survey needs the codegree SMALL relative to the degree (Δ_2 ≤ Δ/(log Δ)^7); on He weights the off-diagonal 'codegree' entries are individually small (max |P_ik|/row-energy = 1.2e-2) but there are n^2 of them: off-diagonal Frobenius energy of (W∘W)W^T is 3n^3(2/n)^3 = 24 against 15n^2(2/n)^3 = 0.117 for the diagonal, ratio n/5 = 205 (CHECKED: 23.91 / 0.1165 = 205.2). This is F2 in miniature: the 'bulk' pairing dominates, and entrywise smallness of codegrees does not make it negligible because the readout sums all of them coherently against the next layer's gates.

mechanisms.name: M3. Nibble with conditional exposure and a quadratic-variation double count
mechanisms.statement: First nibble I_1 is p_1-random with p_1 = γ/Δ (γ ≪ 1), so G[I_1] has average degree γ and is independent after deleting o(|I_1|) vertices; delete D_1 = I_1 ∪ ⋃_{x∈I_1} N(x), a γ-fraction of V, and require that D_1 'looks like' a random set of density γ so that the new max degree and codegree are ≈ (1−γ)Δ; then p_2 = γ/((1−γ)Δ), |I_2| ≈ γ n/Δ; after i nibbles the remaining graph has (1−γ)^i n vertices, the process runs until (1−γ)^i n ≤ n/Δ, i.e. i ≈ (log Δ)/γ steps, giving |I| ≈ (n/Δ) log Δ. Degree control: fix x, condition on x surviving (no neighbour selected), let Y = N(N(x)) \ (N(x) ∪ {x}); expose Y ∩ I_i vertex by vertex, deleting N(v) ∩ X whenever v ∈ Y is selected; concentration follows from a martingale whose increments' squares are controlled by the double-counting inequality (as printed) Σ_{y∈Y} |I ∩ N(y)|^2 ≤ Σ_{y,z∈N(x)} |N(y) ∩ N(z)|, i.e. by codegrees.
mechanisms.where: §3.4 'Sketch proof of Theorem 3.6', pp.11-12, lines 650-696 (double count at lines 692-696).
mechanisms.status: PROVED in [15]; the survey gives the heuristic and the one inequality. The double count itself is an identity: Σ_y |I∩N(y)|^2 = Σ_{z,z'∈I} |N(z)∩N(z')| (CHECKED numerically on a random graph: 2022 = 2022).
mechanisms.relevance_to_F1_F7: The exposure martingale is the same mathematical object as the pinning scheme of sec_problem Cor. directional (ii) (reveal X_i one at a time; the chain's error is minus the sum of the n conditional Jensen gaps), and the 'sum of squared increments' is the quadratic variation d⟨ν⟩_t that enters Theorem defect-path. The Gram theorem (sec_births Thm gram) is exactly the structure 'QV of f(process) = Hessian × Gram of the coordinates' gradients', with Γ_{M_ab M_cd} linking pair (a,b) to (c,d) through one shared covariance entry S_ac — a double count over a shared index like the codegree. This resemblance is exact (it is Itô/chain rule) but it is already in the repo and carries no new estimate. The payoff differs: the survey uses the codegree bound to prove CONCENTRATION of a count (one-sided, o(1) relative accuracy); F5 needs the MEAN of the drift, i.e. the trace Σ_AB ∂²G Γ_AB, exactly to 1e-4 relative (Prop. capacity (iii): 2n+1 chain runs; probes need 1e9 samples). A 'codegree ≪ degree' regime, which would let one drop the off-diagonal Gram, does not exist here: for S = W_1 W_1^T with He rows, ‖S_off‖_F² = n^2·(4/n) = 4n equals ‖diag S‖_F² = n·4 = 4n (PROVED, two lines), so the off-diagonal Gram has the same energy as the diagonal, and F7 says the error is incoherent (collective share 0.2-5%). The nibble's 'remaining graph looks random' requirement has an automatic analogue (Gaussian law stays Gaussian along Eldan's path) and so contributes nothing.

mechanisms.name: M4. Guided constraint-sticking processes: Lovett–Meka walk (Lemma 2.5) and Klartag's evolving ellipsoid
mechanisms.statement: Lemma 2.5 (Lovett–Meka): vectors a^(1..m) with ‖a^(j)‖_∞ ≤ 1, x_0 ∈ [−1,1]^n, c_j ≥ 0 with Σ_j exp(−c_j²/16) ≤ 1/16; then there is x ∈ [−1,1]^n with ⟨x−x_0, a^(j)⟩ ≤ c_j √n for all j and |x_i| = 1 for ≥ n/4 coordinates. Proof: Brownian motion from x_0 that sticks to each hyperplane it hits; 'a random process with mean x_0 and with a covariance matrix that starts as the identity and which is successively projected onto the hyperplanes that it sticks to'; martingale concentration gives P(|⟨X_t−x_0,a^(j)⟩| ≥ c_j√n) ≤ e^{−c_j²/2}, so by t=1 at most 1/16 constraint hyperplanes are hit and many cube facets are. Klartag (Thm 3.4, θ(d) ≥ c d² 2^{−d}): choose a random unimodular lattice Λ, which 'looks locally like a Poisson point process with intensity 1'; grow E_t = {x : ⟨x, A_t x⟩ ≤ 1} (A_t ≻ 0) from a small ball by a random evolution in the ≈ d²/2-dimensional space of ellipsoids; hitting y ∈ Λ 'precisely introduces the linear constraint ⟨y, A_t y⟩ = 1 on A_t' and the ellipsoid keeps y on its boundary; the process stops with ≈ d²/2 lattice points on the boundary, and the Poisson heuristic gives d² ≈ E|E_T ∩ Λ| ≈ Vol(E_T), hence density Vol(E) 2^{−d} = Ω(d² 2^{−d}).
mechanisms.where: Lemma 2.5 and proof sketch: §2.3, pp.6-7, lines 366-404. Klartag: §3.5, pp.12-13, lines 697-733 ('looks locally like a Poisson point process with intensity 1' at lines 710-711; constraint at lines 721-723; volume heuristic at lines 728-733). Survey explicitly links the two: 'a method reminiscent of Lovett and Meka's proof' (line 544) and 'analogous to the proof of Lemma 2.5, although here we are working in the space of ellipsoids' (lines 712-713).
mechanisms.status: PROVED (Lovett–Meka [59]; Klartag [46]); the survey gives heuristics only. The 'locally Poisson of intensity one' statement is the content of Siegel's mean value theorem E|Λ ∩ A \ {0}| = Vol(A); the survey does not name it (my identification).
mechanisms.relevance_to_F1_F7: Verbal, with one structural point. Shared skeleton: both Klartag's volume heuristic and Theorem defect-path rest on a linear functional of a random measure being its first moment (E|E∩Λ| = Vol(E) ↔ u(ν) = ν(F) affine, which makes u(ν_t) a martingale). Beyond that the mechanisms are opposite. Lovett–Meka/Klartag GUIDE a process (sticking to hyperplanes / to lattice points; covariance successively projected) to reach an exponentially unlikely configuration. Eldan's path of Cor. eldan is unguided: ν_t = N(m_t, I/(1+t)) with a deterministic, isotropic covariance and no hitting rule; the directional tilt drives one fixed direction. The question 'would an adaptive, constraint-sticking choice of directions help?' is answered by Prop. capacity and the measurements in sec_capacity: the error is the trace of A = ½H − ∂_Σ E, a k-direction scheme sees Σ_s v_s^T A v_s with SNR √k|δ|/‖A‖_F ≈ 1e-2 √k, and the excess spectrum x_v = ∂_v²e − Δe/n is flat (top direction 5% at n=256, orthogonal to the coherent direction, correlation with the error 0.08-0.26). An adaptive choice of the k best directions would capture at most the top-k eigenvalues of a flat-spectrum matrix, so it cannot resolve a trace; the Eldan path is therefore not 'an adaptive evolving geometry' in Klartag's sense, and making it one would not change Prop. capacity (iii). The projected-covariance structure of the Lovett–Meka walk (I → I − Σ v v^T) is formally the covariance of the directional tilt I − (t/(1+t)) v v^T at t → ∞ (sec_problem Definition), but that scheme is already analysed (Cor. directional (i)) and measures the difference between the chain and its v-localization, not the chain's error.

mechanisms.name: M5. Littlewood–Offord concentration function; classical, inverse and 'typical' theory; LCD and Theorem 4.2
mechanisms.statement: ρ_ε(v) = max_b P(|⟨X,v⟩ − b| < ε), X uniform on {−1,1}^n (line 870; more general X allowed but not treated). Singularity reduction (4.6): P(det B_n = 0) ≤ E_v ρ_0(v) + P(E^c), v the normal to the first n−1 rows. Erdős (1945): all v_i ≠ 0 ⇒ ρ_0(v) ≤ ρ((1,…,1)) = O(n^{−1/2}); Halász: Fourier approach. Inverse theory (Tao–Vu, Nguyen–Vu): if ρ(v) > n^{−C} then O(n^{1−ε}) coordinates are covered by a generalized arithmetic progression of rank O_{ε,C}(1); breaks down when ρ = n^{−ω(1)}. Rudelson–Vershynin LCD: D_α(v) = inf{φ > 0 : d(φ·v, Z^n \ {0}) ≤ √(αn)} (printed '⩽ √αn', line 966); Theorem 4.2: v ∈ S^{n−1}, D_α(v) > c/ε ⇒ P(|⟨X,v⟩| ≤ ε) ≤ Cε + e^{−cαn}. Typical theory (Tikhomirov): for v uniform on S^{n−1} and ε > 2^{−n+o(n)}, E_v ρ_ε(v) = Θ(ε) and P_v(ρ_ε(v) ≥ Lε) ≤ L^{−ω(n)} for large fixed L.
mechanisms.where: §4.1, pp.15-16, lines 866-935; LCD and Theorem 4.2 in §4.2, p.17, lines 962-976.
mechanisms.status: PROVED (cited results: Erdős [26], Tao–Vu [101,99], Nguyen–Vu [64,68], Rudelson–Vershynin [77], Tikhomirov [103]).
mechanisms.relevance_to_F1_F7: The identification 'kink density = concentration function at scale h → 0' is correct only in a restricted sense, PROVED: for the pre-activation z_a with law ν, φ(α_a)/σ_a is the Gaussian closure's value of lim_{h→0} P(|z_a − 0| < h)/(2h), i.e. the concentration function at the FIXED level b = 0, not max_b (the max is attained at b = m_a and equals the mode density 1/(σ√(2π)), which is not the birth strength). CHECKED on net 0 (checkB2, 131072 inputs, window h = 0.1σ): the birth-weighted (count-pooled) true small-ball density at 0 agrees with φ(α)/σ computed from the Monte Carlo (m,σ) to +0.0018/+0.0021/+0.0018/−0.0004 (±0.0005) at layers 3/7/11/15 and to −0.0018 ± 0.0003 at layer 0, the latter being exactly the finite-window bias −h²/(6σ²) = −0.0017 of a Gaussian (z_1 is exactly Gaussian), so the pipeline is calibrated; with the Edgeworth κ3,κ4 correction the pooled agreement is ≤ 1e-3 at every layer. The Gaussian value is 5-8% low for |α| ∈ [2,3) and 15-35% low for |α| ≥ 3 at depth, where births (∝ φ(α)) are negligible. Consequences: (i) the object F6 needs is the VALUE of a smooth density to 1e-4 relative (sensitivity law: 1e-3 relative variance error ⇒ 7× MSE), and the Gaussian/Edgeworth value is right to a few 1e-3 — the percent-level κ3 corrections are already in the chain (sec_transport eq. mean-readout, −αφκ3/(6σ²)); (ii) L–O theory delivers upper bounds with unspecified absolute constants under an arithmetic hypothesis (LCD) on a discrete X, which is the regime the survey itself contrasts with the continuous case: 'v_{[d+1,n]} is a continuous random variable and thus its analysis is vastly easier' (lines 1131-1132). The input here is N(0,I) and the hidden laws are Gaussian with small cumulants; no inverse theorem, LCD or tail estimate says anything at 1e-4 relative precision. The resemblance is verbal.

mechanisms.name: M6. Approximate negative correlation of linear small-ball events: Theorem 4.3
mechanisms.statement: Target shape (4.9): P(|⟨X,v⟩| ≤ ε ∩ ⋂_{i≤k} |⟨X,w_i⟩| ≤ β) ≤ P(|⟨X,v⟩| ≤ ε) P(⋂_i |⟨X,w_i⟩| ≤ β) 'although in an approximate form'; no structure assumed on the w_i, span up to Θ(n). Theorem 4.3: n ∈ N, α ∈ (0,1), 0 ≤ k ≤ αβn, ε ≥ exp(−αβn), v ∈ S^{n−1}, w_1,…,w_k ∈ S^{n−1} orthogonal, X uniform on {−1,1}^n, D_α(v) > 16/ε ⇒ (4.10) P(|⟨X,v⟩| ≤ ε and ⋂_{i=1}^k |⟨X,w_i⟩| ≤ β) < C ε e^{−ck}, C, c absolute. Proof is an O(n)-dimensional Fourier argument in [18], not sketched.
mechanisms.relevance_to_F1_F7: No transfer; hypotheses fail and the Gaussian analogue has the opposite sign. The joint events that appear in the hub pairings are gate/kink products θ_a θ_a θ_c and δ_c (sec_transport Thm transport proof sketch), i.e. joint small-ball/sign events of linear forms of a nearly Gaussian vector; this is the only resemblance. For X ∼ N(0,I) and ⟨v,w⟩ = c, conditioning on |⟨X,w⟩| ≤ β INCREASES the density of ⟨X,v⟩ at 0 by the factor ∫_{−β}^{β} φ(s)φ(−cs/√(1−c²))/(√(1−c²)(2Φ(β)−1)) ds / φ(0) (PROVED by direct computation; CHECKED: 1.048/1.044/1.033/1.010 for c=0.3 and β=0.1/0.5/1/2; 1.249/1.222/1.155/1.035 for c=0.6; 2.278/1.955/1.433/1.048 for c=0.9; Monte Carlo with k=5 orthonormal w_i in n=40, ε=0.05, β=0.5, overlap 0.6: P(A∩B)/(P(A)P(B)) = 1.21). Negative correlation is a discrete/arithmetic phenomenon tied to the LCD condition D_α(v) > 16/ε; nothing in F1-F7 lives on {±1}^n, and the constants C, c are irrelevant at the 1e-4 relative level F5/F6 require.

mechanisms.name: M7. n-dimensional concentration function, rank splitting, and the large-deviation Theorem 4.4
mechanisms.statement: f_ε(v) = P_{A_n}(‖A_n v‖_2 ≤ ε n^{1/2}) for v ∈ S^{n−1} (4.11); Theorem 4.4: for L > 1 and e^{−cn} ≤ ε ≪ 1, P_v(f_ε(v) ≥ (Lε)^n) ≤ (cL)^{−2n}, v uniform on S^{n−1}_♭ (controlled ∞-norm). Weaker form via E_v f_ε(v) ≤ (Cε)^n (4.12) and Markov. Steps: assume v_i = Θ(n^{−1/2}) on d = cn coordinates; replace A_n by the lazy block matrix M (4.14) with H an (n−d)×d µ-lazy ±1 matrix, f_ε(v) ≤ C^n P(‖Mv‖ ≤ εn^{1/2}) (4.13); split by the robust rank event E_k = {σ_{d−k}(H) ≥ c√n, σ_{d−k+1}(H) < c√n} (4.15); use the randomness of H and Theorem 4.3 (tensorized) for P(‖Hv_{[d]}‖ ≤ ε√n ∧ E_k) ≤ (Cεe^{−ck})^{n−d} unless v_{[d]} is structured; use the randomness of v for P_{v_{[d+1,n]}}(‖H^T v_{[d+1,n]}‖ ≤ εn^{1/2}) ≤ (Cε)^{d−k} (4.18) because H^T has at most k small singular directions and v is continuous. The 'reuse of randomness' barrier at exp(−c(n log n)^{1/2}) (lines 799-803) is overcome by controlling both events simultaneously.
mechanisms.status: PROVED in [18]; survey sketches the (cL)^{−n} version.
mechanisms.relevance_to_F1_F7: Verbal only. The split by singular values of a random matrix (E_k) resembles F3's statement that the cocycle T_{l←l'} has 99%-rank > 256 for ages 1-3 and the sec_cost measurement of effective ranks 164, 92, 65, …; but the survey uses the split to bound a probability by a product of per-direction small-ball factors (Cε)^{d−k}, whereas F3's obstruction is that even a correct low-rank truncation of the linear transport does not truncate the Hadamard readout ((QQ^T T)∘(QQ^T T) is not the projection of T∘T). The 'two sources of randomness controlled simultaneously' idea has no counterpart: our weights are fixed (one realization), only the input is random, and the quantity is an expectation, not a tail. Nothing in §4.3 bears on the n^3 memory of F1.

numerical_checks.what: Check A: (i) ((A∘A)A^T)_{ik} equals the codegree |N(i)∩N(k)| for a 0/1 adjacency matrix; (ii) the double-count identity Σ_y |I∩N(y)|² = Σ_{z,z'∈I}|N(z)∩N(z')|; (iii) ensemble statistics of the cubic hub pairing P_l = (W_l∘W_l)W_l^T on the 16 real He matrices of net 0 (W_off0.npy, n=1024): entry means, rms, Frobenius energy off-diagonal vs diagonal, codegree/degree ratio.
numerical_checks.result: (i) max abs diff 0.0; (ii) 2022 = 2022; (iii) E[W²] = 0.00195 = 2/n. Off-diagonal entries: mean 5.0e-5, rms 4.777e-3 (prediction √(3n(2/n)³) = 4.784e-3); diagonal: mean 2.9e-4, rms 1.066e-2 (prediction √(15n(2/n)³) = 1.070e-2); rms of the average over the 16 matrices 1.196e-3 = 4.78e-3/√16, consistent with zero ensemble mean. Frobenius energy per layer: off-diagonal 23.91 (prediction 3n³(2/n)³ = 24; the script's printed label omitted a factor n), diagonal 0.1165 (prediction 15n²(2/n)³ = 0.117), ratio 205.2 = n/5. Max |off-diagonal entry| / mean row energy = 1.2e-2.

numerical_checks.what: Check B: kink density as a small-ball density. Forward pass of 131072 N(0,I) inputs through net 0 (float32, OMP_NUM_THREADS=2, 140 s); at layers 0,3,7,11,15 count |z_a| < 0.1σ_a per neuron and compare the implied density at 0 with φ(α_a)/σ_a from the Monte Carlo (m,σ) and with the Edgeworth density φ(α)/σ·[1 + κ3/(6σ³)He_3(−α) + κ4/(24σ⁴)He_4(−α)]; pooled over neurons (count-weighted, i.e. birth-weighted) and binned by |α|. Sanity: a 65536-input pass reproduced the layer-16 truth means to rms 1.05e-3 against expected MC noise ~7.6e-3.

numerical_checks.what: Check C: sign of the Gaussian analogue of the approximate negative correlation (4.9)/(4.10). Exact 1-D integral of the conditional density of ⟨X,v⟩ at 0 given |⟨X,w⟩| ≤ β for X ∼ N(0,I), ⟨v,w⟩ = c; Monte Carlo with k = 5 orthonormal w_i in n = 40 (4e6 samples).
numerical_checks.result: Conditional/unconditional density at 0: c=0.3: 1.048, 1.044, 1.033, 1.010 for β = 0.1, 0.5, 1, 2; c=0.6: 1.249, 1.222, 1.155, 1.035; c=0.9: 2.278, 1.955, 1.433, 1.048. Monte Carlo (ε=0.05, β=0.5, overlap 0.6 with w_1): P(A∩B)/(P(A)P(B)) = 1.212.
